summary:
We developed FLOWTRACE, an interactive web platform that turns NASA’s BASS/BASS-II combustion data into an accessible investigation of flame survival in microgravity. It combines a functional backend with experiment search, filtering, interactive airflow charts, side-by-side comparisons, and links to NASA evidence.
FLOWTRACE addresses the “Flame in Free Fall” challenge by helping users explore how initial and final airflow, oxygen concentration, and material properties relate to recorded outcomes such as sustained burning, low-flow quenching, and blowoff. Its central investigation uses 31 SIBAL fabric experiments with paired airflow measurements. The platform clearly separates confirmed outcomes from unspecified results, avoiding unsupported predictions.
This project matters because understanding combustion under changing ventilation conditions can inform spacecraft fire-safety research and astronaut protection. Our submission demonstrates how existing NASA data can become a practical, transparent learning and research tool, making complex space-combustion evidence easier for students, researchers, and the public to understand.
details:
Project: Flame in Freefall

What it does and how it works
Flame in Freefall studies how a flame behaves when gravity’s effects are removed. On Earth, a flame is teardrop-shaped because hot gases are lighter and rise, and this buoyancy-driven flow pulls fresh air in from below. In freefall there is no buoyancy, so the flame becomes a small, dim, blue sphere. Oxygen reaches it only by slow diffusion instead of convection. We built a compact drop rig that releases a small combustion chamber with a candle-type flame into freefall. A camera and sensors record the flame as it falls. We then compare its shape, size, color, and burn rate against a ground-based control run under identical conditions. An automated pipeline collects the data and produces the comparison for each run.

Benefits

  • It makes microgravity combustion visible and measurable with low-cost equipment, without a drop tower or spaceflight.
  • It shows clearly that flame behavior depends on gravity-driven airflow, which is often mistaken for a property of fire itself.
  • Automating data collection and comparison makes each experiment repeatable and fast to analyze.

Intended impact
The project aims to make an advanced area of combustion science accessible to students and educators. Fire safety on spacecraft depends on understanding how flames spread in microgravity, where they behave very differently from Earth flames. Our short-term goal is a reproducible, affordable teaching tool. Our longer-term goal is to show that meaningful combustion experiments can be done outside large research facilities.

Tools, languages, hardware, and software

  • Hardware: a sealed combustion chamber, a small flame source, a high-frame-rate camera, a light sensor, an accelerometer to confirm the freefall window, and a microcontroller for timing and release
  • Languages: Python for data analysis and image processing; C/C++ for the microcontroller
  • Software: OpenCV for flame shape and size measurement, n8n to automate data transfer and trigger analysis through webhooks, and plotting libraries for the comparison charts
  • Networking: the rig sends results over the local network to the machine running n8n

How it’s creative
Combustion research in microgravity normally needs drop towers, parabolic flights, or the International Space Station. We reproduce the key phenomenon in a small, affordable setup. The n8n automation layer is also unusual for an experiment like this. It turns a one-off demonstration into a repeatable data pipeline that runs without manual handling.

Factors considered

  • Safety: we used a very small flame in a sealed, fire-safe chamber with a controlled fuel amount and a safe landing system.
  • Freefall duration: the window is short, so camera frame rate and sensor timing were critical.
  • Fair comparison: the ground-based control uses the same chamber, fuel, and camera settings.
  • Reliability: accelerometer data confirms each run was true freefall before it’s included in the analysis.
  • Cost and accessibility: we chose inexpensive, widely available components so others can rebuild it.
  • Data integrity: we added webhook authentication and checks so only valid runs enter the pipeline.
